description: How NVIDIA’s CUDA moat turned a supply-and-demand scramble into a market-share landslide—while AMD’s GPU push and Intel’s turnaround struggled to keep pace.
youtube_description:
🚨 The AI Chip Crown Race: NVIDIA’s CUDA advantage turned a “maybe” into a runaway market-share storm—while Intel’s turnaround and AMD’s ramp fought for every month.

00:00 — 2018: The AI wave is real, but nobody has the crown yet
00:45 — 2019: NVIDIA grows quietly; Intel still dominates corporate budgets
01:40 — 2020: Pandemic-era demand + GPU acceleration starts compounding
02:35 — 2021: The AI gold rush explodes—NVIDIA revenue accelerates fast
03:30 — 2022: Massive AI buildout, shortages, and pricing power (NVIDIA pulls ahead)
04:30 — 2023: AI infrastructure spending hits infrastructure-scale levels
05:20 — 2024: NVIDIA’s leap—AI compute becomes the center of the tech universe
06:10 — 2025: The crown widens; AMD climbs; Intel keeps shedding momentum
07:05 — 2025 inflection: Broadcom/QCOM benefit in adjacent ways, but the GPU throne is different

instagram_caption:
🚀 The AI Chip Crown Race is basically “CUDA vs Everyone”… and the scoreboard is brutal.

In 2018, AI chips were still a bet—most budgets were locked to traditional CPUs, networking, and predictable demand. NVIDIA’s revenue was about $11.72B, Intel was a giant at roughly $70.78B, and AMD sat around $6.64B. The story sounded like “AI is coming,” not “someone is about to dominate everything.”

Then 2020 hit and the world accelerated. As data centers scaled for training and inference, demand for fast GPUs surged. By 2020, NVIDIA rose to about $17.98B and AMD to about $6.48B. Intel, meanwhile, remained huge in absolute terms—around $78.32B—but the momentum started to tilt away from CPUs as AI workloads demanded specialized acceleration.

2021 is where the chart race becomes a sprint. NVIDIA jumped to about $26.92B, while AMD climbed to roughly $15.31B—still far behind, but suddenly in the same arena. Intel peaked near $79.02B (yes, it was still massive), yet the future spending direction was already being rewritten for GPUs and AI platforms.

By 2022, the gap widened: NVIDIA hit about $27.10B, AMD about $17.63B, and Intel slid to around $63.01B. The market wasn’t just buying chips—it was buying ecosystems. NVIDIA’s CUDA software moat and the ability to ship AI infrastructure at scale turned “chip demand” into a compounding flywheel. In 2024, NVIDIA’s revenue jumped to about $61.93B, and by 2025 it reached about $94.00B. AMD rose too (about $28.00B in 2024, ~$35.50B in 2025), but Intel dropped to about $50.60B in 2024 and ~$48.00B in 2025.

So here’s the question: in your view, is this a “software ecosystem wins” story (CUDA), or a “supply + execution” story—and who do you think can meaningfully challenge the crown next: AMD, Intel, or someone new?

Follow for more chart-race timelines. Drop a 🔥 if NVIDIA surprised you most, or an 🧠 if the real twist was Intel’s decline.
facebook_caption:
The AI Chip Crown Race shows how semiconductor momentum increasingly depends on more than silicon. While NVIDIA’s revenue grew from about $11.72B in 2018 to approximately $94.00B by 2025, Intel’s total revenue moved in the opposite direction—roughly $70.78B in 2018, peaking around $79.02B in 2021, then declining to about $48.00B by 2025.

AMD also improved its trajectory, rising from about $6.64B (2018) to ~$35.50B (2025), but it remained behind NVIDIA’s accelerating climb. Adjacent players like Broadcom and Qualcomm benefited from data-center and connectivity demand, yet they did not replace the GPU throne that NVIDIA built around CUDA and large-scale AI infrastructure.

In a world where AI workloads are reshaping compute spending, the chart race makes one thing clear: ecosystems and execution compound faster than traditional hardware cycles.
